t: Find the Number of Good Pairs I
o: We must count pairs (i, j) such that nums1[i] is divisible by nums2[j] * k. In Example 1 (k=1), 1 divides 1; 3 divides 1 and 3; 4 divides 1 and 4 — five good pairs. Example 2: only 12 (= nums1[3]) is divisible by 2*3=6 and 4*3=12, giving 2 pairs. Constraints are tiny (n, m, values ≤ 50), so even brute force over all pairs is instant.
k: With n, m ≤ 50, the O(n*m) double loop is more than fast enough.

a.i: Simply test every combination of i and j. There are at most 2500 pairs, each checked in O(1) with one modulo operation.
s: Loop i over nums1 and j over nums2.

a.n: Approach 2: Count Multiples with a Frequency Table
a.i: Count occurrences of each value in nums1. For each b in nums2, every multiple of b*k up to 50 forms good pairs; add their counts. This trades the pair loop for a divisor-style enumeration.
s: For each b, step through multiples of b*k up to 50 and accumulate freq.
a.t: O(n + m * 50/m) ≈ O(n + 50*m/max_b) — bounded by O(n + 50m)

w: Brute force is perfectly fine here given the constraints; the frequency-table version matters only in the harder follow-up with large arrays. Pitfall: remember k multiplies nums2[j], not nums1[i]. A follow-up might raise n, m to 1e5 — then the counting approach becomes necessary.
